places.name: Neighbourhood houses
places.blurb: Doors shut, curtains drawn. Somebody has to go through the cupboards.

places.name: Pell's bakery
places.blurb: The ovens went cold on the first morning. There are flour sacks in the front and sealed tins in the back.

places.name: The pharmacy
places.blurb: Boarded up the first week. The stock room might still be full.

places.name: The hardware store
places.blurb: Shutter dented, ladder left out. Sheet steel, nails, and shells under the counter.

places.name: St. Aidan's church
places.blurb: The doors stand open and the pews are stacked with coats. Somebody has been keeping the candles lit.

places.name: The fire station
places.blurb: Two bays, and one engine gone. The hose reels, the tank and the locker room are still there.

places.name: Eastgate clinic
places.blurb: Chairs in neat rows and every drawer pulled. The dispensary has a steel door, and someone behind it who has not opened it.

places.name: Millbank terraces
places.blurb: Forty narrow houses in a row, every kitchen the same. A cat lives in number nine and has views on visitors.

places.name: The public library
places.blurb: The reading room is dim and silent, which is how it always was. The staff kitchen is behind the desk.

places.name: The police station
places.blurb: The front doors are chained from the inside. The armoury is at the back, past the cells.

places.name: The crossing fuel stop
places.blurb: A forecourt by the level crossing, a sedan at pump three and the tanks under it not yet dry. The barrier is still down, waiting for a train, and the kiosk shutter is half up.

places.name: Dunne's garage
places.blurb: Two bays, a hoist, and tool cabinets bolted to the floor. A pickup stands on the ramp with its keys on a hook, and the owner kept a shotgun under the till.

places.name: The ring road supermarket
places.blurb: Trolleys piled against the doors, and a car park full of the dead who came to shop. A delivery van sits at the loading bay, and the back shelves were never emptied.

places.name: The scrapyard
places.blurb: A wrecker's yard: crushed cars, sheet metal, a crane that still has its hook. Nothing here is small.

places.name: Ferris radio and TV
places.blurb: Rows of dead screens, and one aerial on the roof turned exactly the right way. Someone upstairs may still be listening.

places.name: The north road truck stop
places.blurb: A café, a shower block and a lorry park, the lorries nose to tail with their tanks full. The drivers' lockers run along the back wall.

places.name: Tern Hill farm
places.blurb: A small hill farm with a root cellar and a hand pump. The gate says 'Stay out, I have a gun', and it is not clear who wrote it.

places.name: The water works
places.blurb: Settling tanks, pump halls, and a chemical store behind a mesh fence. The pumps still run, and nobody is sure what they are pumping.

places.name: The school annex
places.blurb: A prefab block across the river: small chairs, a lunch hall, a nurse's cupboard. The yard fence has been chewed at the bottom.

places.name: The bus depot
places.blurb: Forty buses nose to tail, the windows steamed over from the inside, and the diesel tank by the gate still has some in it. The canteen is at the back, past all of them.

places.name: Larkfield estate
places.blurb: A new estate of identical houses, half of them never lived in. The lived-in half has the cupboards, and its doors have been kicked in.

places.name: The distribution warehouse
places.blurb: A shed the size of a football pitch, pallets to the roof. Most of it is cardboard, and some of it is not.

places.name: The civil defence bunker
places.blurb: A concrete door in a hillside, built for a war that was supposed to be different. The ventilation fans are still turning.

places.name: Hollis farm
places.blurb: A dairy farm at the end of a long lane: grain in the store, a well that works, and a barn door chained from the outside.

places.name: The river bridge
places.blurb: Four lanes of concrete over slow brown water, and cars stopped on it in both directions. The city is on the far side, and nobody has walked back from it.

places.name: The army checkpoint
places.blurb: Sandbags, a barrier arm and a tent with its flaps tied shut. The duty log is still on the table, and its last entry is in capitals.

places.name: Beech Court flats
places.blurb: Six tower blocks round a car park, a lift lobby with a dead man in it, and a lamp lit on the sixth floor every dusk. Somebody up there is still keeping house.

places.name: The harbour cold store
places.blurb: A freezer warehouse on the harbour quay, the power long gone and the smell with it. The dry store upstairs is sealed, and the tins inside are fine.

places.name: St. Bride's hospital
places.blurb: Eleven floors and every window blank in the sun. The pharmacy is in the basement, and so, by the look of the stairs, is most of the staff.

places.name: Kingsmead Mall
places.blurb: Three floors of rolled-down shutters and a fountain full of coins. The food hall was stripped in a week; the supermarket at the back never was.

places.name: Ashgrove University
places.blurb: Lecture halls, a labs block with the chemical store standing open, and a hall of residence barred from the inside. The notice boards still say Freshers' Week.

places.name: The police headquarters
places.blurb: A grey block with a yard full of vans, none of them moved. The firearms store is in the basement behind two steel doors, and one of them is open.

places.name: The Barrow power station
places.blurb: Two cooling towers and a turbine hall, and over the gate a lamp that is still lit. Nobody has found out what is feeding it.

places.name: The airfield fuel depot
places.blurb: A tank farm on the edge of the airfield, bowsers lined up at the loading bays. Whoever shut it down locked it properly, and the keys are somewhere in the admin block.

places.name: Dunmore rail yard
places.blurb: Sidings of wagons nose to tail and a signal box with its windows kicked in. Everything here is steel, and most of it is far too heavy to carry.

beats.text: A loose floorboard in a back bedroom hid a cache of tinned food and a box of shells.
A thin brown dog fell in behind the party and growled at every corner before anyone reached it.
A road atlas lay on the seat of an abandoned van, with four places circled in biro.
Smoke stood on the horizon, and from the next rise the party could see which roofs it was coming from.
A locked pharmacy van stood at the kerb with its keys in the ignition and its shelves untouched.
A woman with a shopping trolley waved the party down a back lane and would take nothing for it.
A warm rain came on, and the party filled every bottle it had under a broken gutter.
A tool chest in a car boot, still locked, held more than the shelves of the shop it was parked outside.
A church bell rang once, a long way off, with nobody at the rope.
A whole roof of crows watched the party go by, and not one of them moved.
Someone had chalked arrows on the pavement, then crossed them out, then drawn more.
A shop window still showed a wedding dress with the price on, new under its coat of dust.
The street was so quiet that the party walked it in single file, listening to its own boots.
A radio in a shop window played one long note until the party was out of earshot.
A shop still held tinned goods, and a dead man behind the counter who stood up when a tin fell.
A climb to a roof cost the party an hour, but it showed three streets nobody had known about.
A bus lay across the road with its doors open, and the way round took an hour.
Someone had been there first: the shelves were bare and the dust on the floor was all disturbed.
A fire had gone through the back of the building, and most of what was left was ash.
A rotten floor gave way under the last of the party, and the fall was longer than it looked.
Something under a parked car caught a boot and would not let go until it had been hit.
A fog came up off the river, and the party sat out two hours in a bus shelter.
The party found a school bag with a name on it and a packed lunch, and nobody spoke for the rest of the walk.
At the level crossing a goods wagon shifted, and what came out of it took one of the party into the dark.
One of the party saw a lit window across the water and went to look, and the others waited until it was too dark to wait.
A lorry had shed its load of nails and glass across both lanes, and getting through, on wheels or on boots, cost an hour.
Somebody had built a roadblock out of cars and pallets, and the way round, through a hedge full of wire, cost an hour and a scratch.
The road ran clear for mile after mile, the sun on the tarmac and not one of the dead in sight, and the party began to talk again.
A lorry stood in a lay-by with its curtain side drawn back on pallets of tins, and not a footprint around it.
Someone had repainted the road signs with the names of what was left, each with an arrow and a tally of who came back.
The queue for the bridge was a mile of cars with their windows up, and the party went down the hard shoulder with the dead watching through the glass.
